strengths: The paper identifies a concrete expressivity limitation in Clifford-Steerable CNNs: for the O(2) vector-vector interaction, the original implicit Clifford kernel construction cannot produce the frequency-2 angular component present in the analytical steerable kernel basis. This is a meaningful and well-motivated observation.

The proposed conditional Clifford-steerable kernel construction is technically natural and useful. Conditioning the implicit kernel network on equivariant statistics of the input field gives a practical way to enrich the kernel while preserving equivariance under the stated conditions.

The theoretical development is mostly clear: the manuscript derives a conditional steerability constraint, states the required equivariance property of the conditioning operator, and connects the implementation to mean pooling as an efficient translation-invariant conditioning mechanism.

The empirical results are promising across several PDE settings, including Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell tasks. The method consistently improves over the original CSCNN in the reported comparisons, which supports the central practical motivation.

The paper discusses an important limitation honestly: full completeness of the conditional kernel basis is only conjectured and left for future work. The future-work discussion on richer conditioning operators is also sensible.
weaknesses: The title and some claims overstate the theoretical result. The manuscript advertises a complete kernel basis, but completeness is only demonstrated heuristically for an O(2) case and then stated as a conjecture for general O(p,q). The empirical evidence does not establish the claimed general completeness.

The implemented conditioning mechanism is much narrower than the general conditional convolution theory. In practice, the kernel is conditioned only on a global masked mean-pooled multivector. This may fail to provide the needed auxiliary directional information in many cases, for example when pooled vector components vanish by symmetry, and the paper does not analyze when conditioning degenerates back to the original CSCNN.

The empirical section lacks important statistical and reproducibility details. The main figures do not report variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; many numerical values are only plotted; hyperparameter selection is described only briefly; and there is no clear code or artifact release statement. This makes it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. The paper says parameter counts are matched except for SWE-5, but the exact parameter counts, tuning budgets, and training protocols for several baselines are not sufficiently detailed. In SWE-5, the proposed large model is not state of the art, underperforming CViT-L and U-F2Net, while the text frames the result somewhat optimistically.

The equivariance validation is limited. Table 2 reports only a layer-level E(2) relative error for Clifford-steerable convolutions, but the paper studies broader O(p,q)/E(p,q) settings, including relativistic spacetime. It would be stronger to test end-to-end equivariance, finite-grid effects, masking effects, and non-Euclidean signature cases.

The presentation has several rough edges, including typographical issues, some unclear notation in proofs, and minor grammatical errors in dataset descriptions. These do not obscure the main idea, but they reduce confidence in the precision of the theoretical exposition.

Limitations and ethics are only lightly treated. The limitations around compute cost, dataset generation artifacts, physical validity of learned rollouts, and possible misuse or failure modes in scientific simulation are not discussed in depth. No major ethical concern is apparent, but the treatment is minimal.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and relevant limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs: the implicit geometric-product kernel construction can miss angular-frequency components in single-layer kernels, with the O(2) vector-vector example giving useful intuition.

The proposed conditioning mechanism is simple and potentially useful: augmenting the kernel network with equivariant input-derived multivectors is a natural way to increase expressivity while preserving the steerability constraint in principle.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad empirical suite across Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell settings, and reports direct comparisons to the original CSCNN as well as several neural PDE baselines.
The authors check numerical equivariance error for the proposed convolution, which is important for this class of method.
weaknesses: The central claim of a complete kernel basis is not established. The title and framing state completeness, but the paper only gives an O(2) motivating example and then explicitly leaves completeness as Conjecture 4.1. This is too large a gap for the main theoretical claim.

The theoretical treatment is underdeveloped and sometimes hand-wavy. Lemma 4.2 relies on saying the conditional kernel network is equivariant 'by definition' and inherits the kernel-head proof from prior work, but the actual representation structure and interaction with multiple conditioning multivectors are not carefully specified. Proposition 4.1 also contains a tautological/typo-like step in Eq. 33, weakening confidence in the proof presentation.

The efficient implementation substantially narrows the proposed operator to global mean-pooling conditioning. This is a mean-field global context signal, not the general conditional convolution initially motivated, and the paper does not convincingly show that it solves the claimed local expressivity limitation in realistic settings rather than merely adding global adaptive parameters.

The empirical evidence is not strong enough to support the broad claims. Results are mostly plotted without exact tables, uncertainty, seeds, statistical variation, or clear training budgets. There is no ablation isolating conditioning from hyperparameter choices, architecture changes, parameter count, pooling mask, normalization, or larger kernel-network capacity.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. SWE-5 uses baseline numbers from prior work with very different parameter counts, while other experiments use mixed families of baselines and limited details. Claims of outperforming state-of-the-art methods are therefore not adequately supported.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper does not provide code availability, full hyperparameters, batch sizes, learning rates, number of epochs/steps, seed protocol, hardware details beyond a partial A100 statement, or enough dataset preprocessing detail to reliably reproduce the results, especially the newly generated relativistic Maxwell dataset.

The paper lacks a serious limitations and ethics discussion. It mentions future work on conditioning operators, but does not discuss failure modes, computational cost, limitations of global pooling, finite-grid equivariance issues, sensitivity to boundary/masking choices, or risks from simulation-generated data assumptions.

Presentation quality is uneven, with typos, notation inconsistencies, malformed equations/snippets, and figure/table reporting that makes it hard to audit the empirical claims. These issues are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the exact method and evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a concrete expressivity limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs: the kernel basis can miss angular frequency components, illustrated for the O(2,0) vector-vector interaction. This is a meaningful technical issue for equivariant PDE models rather than a cosmetic modification.

The proposed conditional Clifford-steerable convolution is conceptually clean. Conditioning the implicit kernel on equivariant summaries of the input feature field is a natural way to enrich the kernel network while preserving the equivariance constraint, and the paper derives the relevant conditional steerability condition.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this research area, covering Navier-Stokes, shallow-water equations, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell tasks, and comparing to CSCNNs plus several neural PDE solver baselines.

The results suggest consistent improvements over the original CSCNN, often with clear data-efficiency gains. The equivariance-error experiment also supports the claim that the implemented conditional layer preserves equivariance up to numerical precision.
The manuscript is generally readable and well motivated, with useful appendices describing proofs, implementation choices, datasets, and additional results.
weaknesses: The strongest claim in the title and abstract, that the method provides a complete kernel basis, is not actually proven. The paper formulates completeness as a conjecture and provides only an O(2,0)-motivated argument plus empirical evidence. This should be framed more cautiously.

The theoretical analysis is somewhat narrow relative to the generality claimed. The incompleteness and recovery arguments are mostly built around O(2,0), while the method is presented as broadly applicable to arbitrary pseudo-Euclidean groups O(p,q).

The conditioning used in the practical implementation is a global mean-pooled multivector, which is much less expressive than the general conditional convolution introduced earlier. The paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of when this mean-field conditioning is sufficient and when it may fail.

Experimental reporting is positive but not fully convincing. Several key results are shown only in plots without exact numerical tables, and the SWE-5 comparison uses models with very different parameter counts and partly externally sourced baselines, making the strength of the state-of-the-art comparison harder to judge.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone. The appendices describe architectures at a high level, but many training hyperparameters, tuning procedures, seeds, exact baseline configurations, code availability, and compute/runtime costs are missing or underspecified.

The paper under-discusses computational tradeoffs. It states that mean-pooling conditioning has negligible additional cost, but does not provide wall-clock time, memory use, or throughput comparisons, which are important for PDE solvers and equivariant CNNs.

Limitations and ethics are thin. The future-work paragraph mentions alternative conditioning operators, but the paper does not sufficiently discuss limitations of the completeness conjecture, finite-grid equivariance violations, benchmark scope, or possible failure modes in scientific modeling applications.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete expressivity limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs and proposes a technically natural extension: conditioning the implicit Clifford-steerable kernel on equivariant summaries of the input field. The conditional equivariance constraint and the mean-pooling implementation are clearly motivated and mostly well integrated with the existing CSCNN framework.

The empirical gains over the direct CSCNN baseline are consistent and substantial across several PDE tasks: Navier-Stokes, shallow-water, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell. The method is especially compelling on fluid dynamics tasks, where it outperforms strong baselines under matched parameter budgets.

The paper includes useful ablations on the conditioning operator and reports equivariance error and inference time. The finding that mean conditioning adds negligible overhead relative to CSCNNs is practically important.

The limitations section is unusually honest: it acknowledges the lack of a general completeness proof, finite-grid equivariance issues, simple conditioning operators, and inherited restrictions of multivector field types. The impact statement is reasonable and does not overclaim major ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim about recovering kernel-basis completeness is not fully established. The paper provides an O(2,0) argument and then states a broader conjecture for O(p,q), but some wording in the abstract/conclusion suggests the limitation is generally remedied. The evidence supports improved expressivity, not a general completeness theorem.

The conditioning used in the efficient implementation is a global mean-field summary, which is much less expressive than the general conditional convolution introduced theoretically. The paper does not sufficiently analyze when this global conditioning is informative, for example when physical fields have near-zero means or when local/nonlocal structure matters.

The ablation with a fixed random condition is concerning: it performs close to equivariant mean/max conditioning while not preserving equivariance. This weakens the argument that the observed gains are specifically due to principled equivariant input-dependent conditioning rather than simply adding extra degrees of freedom or symmetry-breaking basis elements.

Experimental reliability is limited by missing uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or statistical tests. The reported improvements are often large, but for a main-track ML paper the absence of variance is a reproducibility and evidence weakness, especially across many baselines and dataset-size settings.

The SWE-5 scaling comparison uses results from prior work with models of very different sizes and likely different training protocols. This is useful context but not a fully controlled comparison, so claims about being on par with state of the art should be softened.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The paper gives architecture and dataset descriptions, but does not provide a clear code release, exact hyperparameter tables for all baselines, random seeds, training budgets, or enough detail to regenerate the new relativistic Maxwell dataset reliably.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are several technical and writing rough edges, including minor notation inconsistencies, typos, and proof sketches that rely on statements such as the equivariance of the kernel head without enough detail for a self-contained verification.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete expressivity limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs and proposes a plausible, simple extension: conditioning the implicit kernel network on equivariant summaries of the input feature field. This is a meaningful direction for PDE surrogate modeling.

The conditional equivariance constraint is derived clearly at a high level, and the mean-pooling construction is a reasonable way to retain parameter sharing while adding input-dependent kernel expressivity.

The empirical comparison against standard CSCNNs is consistently favorable across several PDE benchmarks. The reported gains over the direct baseline are large, and the inference-time ablation suggests the mean-conditioning mechanism adds negligible overhead.
The manuscript includes limitations, an ablation over conditioning operators, inference timing, and dataset descriptions, which are useful for assessing the scope of the contribution.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is over-stated. The paper argues that conditioning restores missing kernel bases, but the evidence is mostly an O(2) illustrative algebra/code argument and then a conjecture for general O(p,q). The conclusion and limitations sometimes imply a stronger completeness result than is actually proven.

The proposed mean-pooled conditioning only helps if the pooled multivector supplies informative independent directions; this is not guaranteed. For fields with zero or uninformative global mean, the claimed recovery of angular components may fail, and the paper does not characterize when the mechanism is actually expressive enough.

The equivariance story is not fully convincing in the implemented setting. The theory assumes equivariant/translation-invariant conditioning, but the finite grid, cropping, circular masking, and boundary effects complicate exact E(p,q)-equivariance. The reported equivariance check is narrow: single-layer, one dataset, one error metric, and no detailed transformation protocol.

The experimental evidence lacks statistical rigor. Tables report single numbers without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or seed variation, despite relatively small datasets and many baselines. This makes it hard to judge whether some gains, especially against strong baselines, are robust.

Reproducibility is weak. Hyperparameters are described mostly by reference to prior work or vague statements such as training to convergence; optimizer schedules, batch sizes, epoch counts, seeds, model selection, and baseline tuning details are insufficient. Code availability is not stated.

The comparisons to state-of-the-art methods are only partly persuasive. Some baselines appear reimplemented while others are taken from prior papers, and SWE-5 compares models with very different parameter counts and possibly different training/evaluation protocols. Claims of being on par with state of the art are therefore somewhat inflated.

The random-conditioning ablation performs surprisingly close to equivariant mean/max conditioning, which weakens the interpretation that the gains come specifically from principled equivariant conditioning or restored kernel completeness. This deserves deeper analysis.

Presentation is generally readable but contains several imprecise or inconsistent claims, typographical issues, and occasional mismatches between what is proved, conjectured, and empirically suggested. The paper would benefit from more careful separation of theorem, conjecture, and empirical observation.

The impact statement is brief and mostly generic. Ethical risks are likely limited, but the paper does not discuss possible misuse or failure modes of learned physical simulators beyond saying no direct negative consequences are foreseen.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful extension of Clifford-Steerable CNNs by conditioning the implicit kernel on equivariant summaries of the input field. The idea is simple, compatible with the existing CSCNN framework, and addresses a concrete expressivity limitation in prior work.

The theoretical development is largely well motivated: the manuscript derives an equivariance constraint for conditional steerable convolutions and explains why adding auxiliary multivectors can recover missing angular dependence in the O(2,0) case.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area, covering Navier-Stokes, shallow-water equations, 3D Maxwell, and relativistic Maxwell tasks, with comparisons to CSCNNs, Clifford/steerable ResNets, neural operators, Transolver, CViT, and other strong baselines.

The results are consistently favorable relative to standard CSCNNs, often by large margins, and the method is competitive with state-of-the-art baselines while adding almost no inference overhead over CSCNN in the reported Maxwell timing experiment.
The paper includes useful ablations of the conditioning operator, an explicit equivariance-error check, dataset descriptions, architecture details, limitations, and an impact statement.
weaknesses: The strongest theoretical claim is not fully established. The paper only gives a concrete O(2,0) argument and leaves general completeness for O(p,q) as a conjecture, yet parts of the presentation and conclusion suggest broader completeness more strongly than is proven.

The O(2,0) completeness evidence is also more illustrative than rigorous: symbolic products showing the presence of higher-frequency terms do not by themselves prove that the full analytical steerable kernel basis can be represented with the proposed architecture under finite width/depth and actual parameterization constraints.

Some equivariance claims around conditioning operators need more care. Mean pooling is plausible, but the statement that max pooling preserves equivariance for multivector/vector-valued features is questionable unless the pooling operation is defined in a representation-compatible way; componentwise max generally does not commute with rotations.

The experimental evidence is strong against CSCNNs, but less decisive for broad state-of-the-art claims. On the Maxwell tasks Transolver is clearly better, and on SWE-5 the large C-CSCNN trails CViT-L and U-F2Net, so the method is best characterized as competitive rather than uniformly state of the art.

Reproducibility is only moderate from the manuscript alone. The appendix gives architecture and dataset details, but key training hyperparameters, random seeds, variance/error bars, exact splits, and code availability are not sufficiently specified for reliable independent replication.

The evaluation would be strengthened by statistical uncertainty across multiple runs and by more systematic analysis of parameter/compute tradeoffs, especially because several SWE-5 baselines are taken from prior work and differ substantially in architecture and parameter count.

The limitations discussion is honest but could better address practical constraints: CSCNN-style Clifford operations remain much slower than ordinary CNNs, exact equivariance is weakened on finite grids, and global mean conditioning may be too weak for nonlocal or spatially heterogeneous dynamics.
